newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE - Turkish economic pains persist under Erbakan rule.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turkish economic pains persist under Erbakan rule.

text.p: The failure of Turkey's troubled Islamist-led government to ease pressure on the fragile economy has made the realisation of 1997 macro-economic targets increasingly unlikely, analysts say.

Despite three revenue-raising packages, aimed at plugging the hole in public finances, the economy is struggling with high inflation, widening trade and budget deficits and waning international credibility.

Last week, Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan admitted for the first time his government's target of a balanced 1997 budget was in trouble. The budget showed a deficit in 1996 of 1,217 trillion lira ($9 billion), more than eight percent of gross national product (GNP).

Erbakan blamed the budget difficulties on an "artificial political crisis" -- a reference to a row with the military over Islamist activism which has put in doubt the future of his coalition with conservatives.

He said previously the budget was in surplus in the first two months of the year. But economists said that was only a result of accounting tricks and estimated the total first quarter deficit at more than 300 trillion lira ($2.2 billion).
Moreover, they say the balanced budget aim, based on an assumption that more privatisation revenue would be transferred to the budget, was unrealistic and ill-structured.

A projected budget income of $4.5 billion from the sale of licences and shares in Turk Telekom appears endangered after senior privatisation and company officials said the deal was unlikely to take place this year.
Economists predicted that the end-1997 budget deficit might exceed 1,500 trillion lira ($11 billion) and the government may have to prepare a mini-budget to deal with it.
INFLATION TARGET MAY BE REVISED UP
The weaker than programmed budget performance will probably force the government to revise up its 1997 inflation target of 57 percent, officials say.
Wholesale prices have climbed 25.6 percent so far this year after a rise of 84.9 percent in the whole of 1996.
"We expect the end-1997 wholesale price inflation to stand at 72.8 percent," said Altug Karamenderes, an economist at Ata Securities. Estimates ranged between 72 and 80 percent.
Economists say inflation will remain high unless Turkey brings down its huge public sector borrowing requirement, which stood at 9.4 percent of GNP last year.
PRIVATISATION STILL STAGNANT
Analysts say Ankara must rein in borrowing levels by curbing the losses of pension funds and state firms while speeding up sell-offs. Privatisation has brought in only $23 million in cash this year.
The ongoing political crisis has put privatisation plans on hold. The decision-making Higher Board of Privatisation has not met since March 29.
The Privatisation Administration (OIB) had aimed to conclude $4.5 billion worth of deals this year. Even some OIB officials, however, believes the target is over-optimistic.
The OIB has completed deals worth $553 million so far.
Another batch worth $463 million is still in the pipeline, waiting for approval from the Board which consists of four senior cabinet ministers and the OIB chairman under Erbakan's presidency.
"Looking at the present pace of privatisation, it will be very optimistic to say the OIB will complete $2 billion worth of privatisation this year," said an OIB official, who declined to be named.
EXTERNAL DEFICITS GROWING
The lack of success at home is increasing pressures on the government to raise more funds abroad to finance deficits.
But the picture is not very encouraging for Erbakan.
The foreign trade deficit widened 12.6 percent to $2.6 billion in the first two months of this year, signalling that the 1997 target of $20.5 billion would be overshot.
That might also endanger the government's 1997 current account deficit target of $5.6 billion and increase Turkey's dependence on foreign borrowing to finance the shortfall.
"But the government is not very flexible in foreign borrowing," said a former central banker.
"According to the feedback we gathered from foreigners, the sentiment towards Turkey is becoming negative, particularly in the Japanese and U.S. markets," he added.
Turkey's speculative gradings from leading rating agencies appear to be a major factor in restraining efforts to tap international borrowing markets at reasonable rates.
Under these constraints, Ankara has been acting as a net foreign debt repayer for years. The Treasury will service around $8 billion of foreign debt this year.

On the borrowing side, it issued two sets of Eurobonds -- a 500 million mark and a 300 Italian lire issue -- in the first quarter of this year. Officials say plans for a third Euro issue of $250 million, has been delayed because of volatility in the U.S. Treasuries market.
The borrowing figure might go up further with project loans to be acquired from international bodies and governments but it will not be enough to cover annual debt repayments.

To overcome the impasse, Erbakan has tried to attract savings of residents and Turks living abroad under a tax-free import scheme. His government has raised 1.97 billion marks through the scheme -- about 48 percent from abroad and 52 percent from residents of Turkey.
FINANCIAL MARKETS STABLE UNDER CENTRAL BANK GRIP
Despite alarming economic indicators and political instability, financial markets have remained stable under the central bank's tight grip.

"The central bank now controls the money market through its monetary policies. I think interest rates might ease in coming days due to the central bank's control on liquidity and fading political tension," said Erdogan Cicek, treasurer of EGS Bank.

Political uncertainty, fuelled by Erbakan's reluctance to implement anti-Islamist measures and intensified opposition efforts to topple the government, sent stocks down about five percent last week. Money market rates rose 10 percentage points to an average 90 percent from 80 percent in the same period.
The tension has eased since Erbakan's coalition partner, Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, pledged to stand by him last week. ($1 = 135,500 Turkish lira)
